summary: A framework document that classifies the approaches and issues for running IP over ATM networks, to help focus the IP over ATM working group. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Two different kinds of networks needed to work together. This is a map of the choices and problems, so the group could decide where to start.

questions: how does ip run over atm
what are the issues with ip over atm
subtitle: Framework for choosing how to run IP networks on top of ATM infrastructure.

tldr.problem: ATM networks are fundamentally different from traditional IP networks, and there are multiple ways to run IP on top of ATM. The community needed to understand the different approaches and their trade-offs.
tldr.mechanism: This framework classifies IP over ATM approaches by encapsulation (how IP packets are wrapped), connection model (connection-oriented vs connectionless), address resolution (static or dynamic), and routing strategy. It describes the key proposals under discussion and shows how they differ.
tldr.outcome: The framework helped the IP over ATM working group understand the landscape of options and focus effort on the most promising approaches. Different proposals work better for different network sizes and topologies.

facts.label: Main purpose
facts.value: Framework for IP over ATM approaches

today: RFC 1932 is an Informational framework document from 1996. Although ATM technology never became as ubiquitous as some expected, the framework's principles remain relevant to any scenario where connectionless and connection-oriented technologies must work together. Modern technologies like MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) address similar design questions about how to layer different network models.

sections.title: Why IP Needs ATM
sections.content:
ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) is a network technology based on establishing dedicated connections (virtual circuits) between endpoints. IP (Internet Protocol) is a connectionless technology that treats each packet independently and routes it to its destination. These two approaches are fundamentally different: ATM connections are set up first and then used to carry data, while IP routes each packet on the fly.

ATM offers significant advantages, including guaranteed quality of service and efficient multiplexing of many connections. However, IP is the world's dominant protocol and likely to remain so. Organizations want to use ATM's benefits while running IP. The problem is there are multiple ways to do this, each with different implications for performance, complexity, and scalability.
sections.eli5: ATM and IP are different post office systems. They have different strengths. This RFC helps people figure out how to use them together.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
To run IP over ATM, several decisions must be made. First, encapsulation: how are IP packets wrapped for transport over ATM? Options range from LLC/SNAP (a standard wrapping that labels the protocol type), to VC multiplexing (attaching each protocol directly to a virtual circuit), to specialized formats like TULIP and TUNIC that eliminate IP header overhead.

Second, connection management: should a new ATM connection be created for each traffic flow, or should multiple flows share a single connection? This involves a trade-off: dedicated connections allow per-flow quality of service but consume connection resources. Shared connections conserve resources but may not guarantee quality of service.

Third, address resolution: how are IP addresses mapped to ATM addresses? In a LAN (Logical IP Subnet), all systems are supposed to be able to communicate directly with each other. For ATM, this mapping can be static (configured by hand) or dynamic (learned automatically).

Fourth, routing: how do routers determine paths through ATM networks? Classical IP routing treats ATM as just another link. Some proposals try to exploit ATM's connection-oriented nature more fully.
sections.eli5: How do you wrap the mail? How many packages per truck? How do you know whose address is whose? And how do you decide which roads to use?

sections.title: Encapsulation Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC describes several encapsulation approaches. LLC/SNAP is the default: IP packets are wrapped in an LLC/SNAP header that identifies the protocol type, and multiple different protocols can share a single virtual circuit. This is flexible but adds overhead.

VC multiplexing (or Null Encapsulation) eliminates the LLC/SNAP header but requires a dedicated virtual circuit for each protocol pair (IP, ARP, etc.). This reduces overhead but requires more virtual circuits.

TULIP (TCP and UDP over Lightweight IP) assumes direct reachability and eliminates most of the IP header overhead for data packets. The connection setup phase binds the source and destination addresses, so the actual data packets only need to carry the protocol field. This is very efficient but assumes single-hop reachability.

TUNIC (TCP and UDP over a Nonexistent IP Connection) goes further, eliminating even the IP protocol field by binding directly at the application level (e.g., TCP to ATM). This provides maximum efficiency but requires application-level support.
sections.eli5: You can wrap the package with a detailed label, use a simpler label, or get so clever that you barely need any label at all.

sections.title: Connection-Oriented vs Connectionless
sections.content:
ATM is connection-oriented: you set up a virtual circuit first, then use it. IP is connectionless: you send each packet independently. The key question is how tightly to couple IP flows to ATM virtual circuits.

A pure connection-oriented approach creates a new ATM virtual circuit for each traffic flow. This allows each flow to get its own quality of service parameters and guarantees. However, setting up and tearing down connections costs resources and time, especially for short-lived traffic like DNS queries.

A pure connectionless approach runs all IP traffic over a few (or one) shared ATM virtual circuits and lets IP handle congestion management. This conserves connection resources but loses the ability to give quality of service to individual flows.

A middle ground approach uses a signaling protocol (such as RSVP) to indicate when quality of service is needed. Only traffic that requests it gets a dedicated virtual circuit. Other traffic shares a default circuit. This offers the best of both worlds for many scenarios.
sections.eli5: You can dedicate a whole truck to each package. Share one truck among many packages. Or decide per package based on how important it is.

sections.title: Routing and Address Resolution
sections.content:
IP routing normally divides networks into subnets. Routers handle traffic between subnets; hosts communicate directly with other hosts in their own subnet. For large ATM networks, creating a single IP subnet is impractical because subnet management (especially address resolution) does not scale well.

The challenge is that ATM can support direct connections between any two systems (not just those on the same subnet), so it would be beneficial to create direct ATM connections across subnet boundaries. This requires address resolution (mapping IP addresses to ATM addresses) across subnets and requires routing protocols to coordinate these shortcuts.

The RFC describes several proposals: the Classical IP model treats ATM as a LAN substitute and uses separate subnets with routers between them. The NHRP (Next Hop Resolution Protocol) lets hosts discover direct paths across subnet boundaries and set up direct ATM connections. The Peer Model tries to merge ATM and IP addressing. The Integrated Model combines IP routing with ATM routing to provide timely information about available shortcuts.
sections.eli5: You can treat ATM like a regular network and use routers between different areas. Or you can let people discover shortcuts to each other directly.

sections.title: Use Cases and Scalability
sections.content:
Different approaches suit different network sizes and administrative structures. For a corporate LAN, a single large IP subnet over ATM with classical proxy ARP might work well. For a large service provider network, separate IP subnets connected by routers might be necessary, possibly with protocol extensions to enable shortcuts.

The RFC emphasizes that there is no single right answer. Small networks might benefit from simpler approaches that assume ATM everywhere. Large networks like the Internet need approaches that work in a mixed environment with both ATM and non-ATM links. Networks with a single administrator can use simpler approaches than networks where multiple organizations must cooperate.

The framework's main contribution was helping the working group understand these choices and focus on approaches most likely to scale and interoperate. The fact that different proposals make different trade-offs is not a problem; rather, it reflects the real diversity of network environments where IP over ATM might be deployed.
sections.eli5: A small office's one truck network is very different from the nationwide postal system. This framework helps each kind of network find the right approach.
